title: These Headphones Add Sound. Why Does It Go Quiet? | How It Works #8
simplified: Simplified model: one outside microphone, one chip and one speaker shown; real headphones also use a microphone inside the cup and passive padding. Waves are drawn as clean sine waves; real hum is messier. Meter is illustrative, no dB values.

hook_candidates.text: These headphones add sound. So why does the hum disappear?
hook_candidates.note: 'disappear' is too strong: ANC cuts low hum a lot but not to zero

hook_candidates.text: These headphones add sound. So why does it go quiet?
You put these on and the engine hum fades. They're making noise.
Watch this meter. Adding a second sound has to make it fall.
Noise plus noise equals quiet. How?

parts.text: So why does it go quiet?
It has to reach the quiet line.
and a chip plays its mirror image.
and they stack. The hum gets louder.
A voice wiggles too fast to copy,

sources: Microphones pick up outside noise: 'Microphones pick up noise outside of the earpiece.' Sennheiser support, 'What is Active Noise Cancelling', https://support.sennheiser-hearing.com/hc/en-at/articles/34973151457565-What-is-Active-Noise-Cancelling (read 2026-11-28). Sonos: 'Headphones with ANC use tiny microphones inside the ear cups to continuously analyze the sound', https://www.sonos.com/en-us/blog/how-does-noise-canceling-work

Opposite-phase wave cancels: 'The headphones' electronics create a sound wave with the opposite phase and play it back in the earpiece.' 'When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out.' (Sennheiser, as above). Sonos: 'create a soundwave that's the exact opposite.'

Physics of cancelling and stacking: two identical waves 180 degrees out of phase give zero amplitude; in phase they add to twice the amplitude; resultant amplitude 2A cos(phi/2). OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 16.5 Interference of Waves, https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/16-5-interference-of-waves. 'Timing wrong -> louder' follows from this: anti-noise with a timing (phase) error delta gives |2A sin(delta/2)|, larger than the noise alone when delta exceeds 60 degrees; the video shows a large error.

Voices get through: 'Active noise cancellation works best for repetitive, low-frequency noises' and 'It is less effective for higher-frequency sounds like people talking.' (Sennheiser, as above). Sonos: 'ANC excels at blocking low-frequency sounds, like the hum of an airplane or drone of an engine.'
'Near silence' is for the steady low hum only, and is illustrative; the meter shows no dB value. Sennheiser: 'The noise doesn't disappear - you just don't register it.'
comment_question: Have you ever taken noise-cancelling headphones off on a plane or bus and been shocked how loud it was?
